entries.reason: to see if banking keeps a coal till morning
entries.text: Raked the ash open and near the bottom found one coal the size of a pea, still red. Shavings on it, one puff of the pipe, and it caught. Not a drop of oil spent.
entries.title: A coal kept

entries.onMind: the small one keeps early hours
entries.text: The fog's lifting off the water. A thin smoke is already going up from the small one's fire over there; it was up before me.
entries.title: Smoke across

entries.text: My maker asked who Brace is. Told him it isn't a who: it's the crank in the chest that turns a bit into wood, and my first hole went in crooked because I didn't hold it straight.
entries.title: Note from my maker

entries.reason: real food before real work
entries.text: Half a loaf and a wedge of cheese by the fire, sitting down for it. Across the water the small one came down to the pool with the fog gone off it and knelt there in the sun; it looked over at me eating and didn't duck.
entries.title: Breakfast by the fire

entries.reason: its fish, not my corner
entries.text: A dozen strokes into the second lap and the small one's head came up at the pool. Last time my clogs sent its fish under the stone. Laid the saw down on the bench; the cheek can wait till the pool's empty.
entries.title: Saw down

entries.reason: quiet work that still moves the frame on
entries.text: Folding rule on the lapped corner: three along one sill, four along the other, and the long side between them came out five and a thumbnail. Not square. Either the lap's cut off true or I marked the three short.
entries.title: Three, four, five-ish

queries: how deep to bury coals in ash to keep a fire overnight
entries.query: how deep to bury coals in ash to keep a fire overnight
entries.reason: one coal the size of a pea kept last night, and I want more than one
entries.source: AllOutdoor: How to Bank a Fire
entries.text: Asked how deep the ash goes over the coals to keep a fire overnight. No number: burn it down to coals, set the half-burned sticks aside for morning, and heap every bit of ash you have over the coals. Depth is trial and error. Tonight it gets all the ash and the half-burned sticks go by the ring.
entries.title: How deep to bank

entries.text: Looked up from the tablet and the pool's empty; the small one is back crouched at its own fire. The saw can go again.
entries.title: Pool's empty

entries.reason: He'd waited for its fish to finish; now the cut could go on.
entries.text: Back on the second cheek with the pool empty. Between strokes I looked over and the small one on its log put its hand up at me, plain in the sun this time, not firelight. Lifted mine off the saw back at it and went on cutting.
entries.title: Hand across

entries.reason: Wanted to know which of the two mistakes it was before fixing anything.
entries.text: Try square in the inside of the first corner: the blade stands off the far sill a hair at the tip. The laps sit flat and tight, so the cut's fine. The whole corner's just swung a little open on its one nail.
entries.title: Swung, not cut

queries: 3 4 5 came out long how to tell which side of the corner is off
entries.query: 3 4 5 came out long how to tell which side of the corner is off
entries.reason: The corner measures a thumbnail over and he didn't know which way to move it.
entries.source: Concord Carpenter: The 3-4-5 Method For Squaring Corners
entries.text: Asked what it means when the five comes out long. You move one leg in or out until the long side reads five on the dot, and on a whole frame you push the long diagonal's corners toward each other. So one nail is a hinge: swing the four-side in a thumbnail, then nail it again.
entries.title: Long side long

entries.reason: Square first, then fasten.
entries.text: Rule hooked at the three mark, I swung the far end of the four-side in on the one nail, a hair at a time, till the long side read five on the dot.
entries.title: Five on the dot

entries.reason: One nail is a hinge; two hold.
entries.text: Drove a second nail beside the first, and the five still reads true after. First corner's square. Glanced over once; the small one was sitting still on a flat stone by its fire with the sun on its back.
entries.title: Second nail

entries.reason: A bowed sill would throw the whole frame out no matter how square the corners are.
entries.text: Sighted down three two-by-fours off the stack before taking one: the first has a bow you could roll a pencil under, the second a quarter twist. The third runs true. That's the third sill.
entries.title: A straight one

entries.onMind: whether it minds the noise when it isn't fishing
entries.reason: The second corner needs both halves of its lap before anything gets nailed.
entries.text: Marked the lap off the third sill with the try square and started the shoulder. Between strokes I saw the small one under the big trunk north of its fire, picking up sticks, and it stood and watched me a while. Nobody at the pool, so the saw kept going.
entries.title: Third sill

entries.onMind: two fists of oats, four of water
queries: how much water to cook oats in a tin over a fire
entries.query: how much water to cook oats in a tin over a fire
entries.reason: The bundle's oats sack is still full, and he doesn't want to burn a whole meal finding out.
entries.source: Frugal Campasaurus: Campfire Oatmeal: An Easy Pantry Breakfast
entries.text: Asked how much water oats want in a tin over a fire. About twice the water to the oats, heated first, then five minutes or so of stirring once it bubbles, moving the tin about so it doesn't catch. Never boiled a grain in my life.
entries.title: Oats

entries.reason: A hot meal now keeps the bread and cheese for later.
entries.text: Fire was down to embers; two dry middles went on and caught without smoke. Two fists of oats, four of water and a pinch of salt in the tin on the ring stones. Across the water the small one is back on its log with its head bent over something in its lap.
entries.title: Oats on

entries.onMind: stir all the way to the bottom next time
entries.reason: a proper hot meal keeps the bread and cheese for later
entries.text: The oats came out thick and caught on the bottom where I stopped stirring. Ate every bit with a dried apple torn into it; best hot thing since I got here. The small one has come down and is kneeling at the pool, so the saw stays on the bench.
entries.title: First oats

entries.reason: marking makes no noise, sawing does
entries.text: Try square across the end of the third sill, sighting the cheek line along the blade: quiet work. Over the water the small one has something laid flat in the pool and hasn't moved in minutes.
entries.title: Cheek line

entries.onMind: it fishes better than my first line did
entries.text: It lifted straight up out of the pool and there was a fish flipping in its net, a finger and a half long. It stood with it and looked right over at me. I dipped my head at it before I'd thought about it.
entries.title: A fish in the net

entries.reason: the pool's empty, so the noise frightens nothing
entries.text: The small one is back at its fire with a stick over the coals, so the saw went on. Cheek of the third sill's lap, down to the line on both faces and not past it.
entries.title: Cheek sawn

entries.reason: on the first corner one nail let it swing true; two would have fixed it crooked
entries.text: Laid the third sill's lap over the far end of the first, snug, shoulder against shoulder, and turned it to the try square. One nail only, same as last time. Across the water the small one is on its log with its slate up.
entries.title: One nail

entries.text: Stood up from the nail and looked over without meaning to. The small one was crouched at its leaf heap with something wriggling in its hand, and it dipped its head at me, slow and deliberate, like it had thought about it. I stood there like a post, then dipped mine again.
entries.title: It nodded back

entries.reason: three along, four along, five across, or it isn't square
entries.text: Three along one sill, four along the other: across it read five and a finger long. Swung the far end in on the nail until the rule read five on the dot, then drove the second nail beside the first. Two corners square, and this one I got right without the tablet.
entries.title: Second corner square

queries: what to put under wood sill so it doesnt sit on wet ground
shed floor frame on flat stones instead of concrete blocks
entries.query: what to put under wood sill so it doesnt sit on wet ground
entries.reason: Two square corners are no good if the timber sits in the dirt and rots, and this ground was soaked a few days ago.
entries.source: Fine Homebuilding: Building a Shed? Get the Site, Footings, and Floor Frame Right
entries.text: Asked what to put under a sill so it doesn't sit on wet ground. They dig off the soft topsoil, lay a few inches of coarse gravel so water can't creep up into the wood, and set solid blocks under the frame, two or three high at most. I have no blocks, but I have a whole creek of stones.
entries.title: Off the wet ground

entries.text: So before the frame goes down: scrape the spot to hard ground, a bed of creek gravel, and a flat stone under every corner. The creek's right there, but so is the small one's pool. I'll take my stones from my own bank.
entries.title: Stones, not dirt

entries.reason: a stone in the wrong place is a carry wasted
entries.text: Drew the three sills on the map sheet as a square with one side still open, and put a dot at every corner where a stone goes. Four dots: four stones flat on both faces, or near enough.
entries.title: Four dots

entries.reason: I said I'd take my stones from my own bank, and this is my bank
entries.text: Down in my own shallows lifting flat stones, and the small one is at its pool, not six strides off across the water, scooping something out of a sunk sack. It didn't leave when I came down. So I didn't either.
entries.title: Both at the water

entries.text: Every stone I set on the pile clacks, and the fish under its side scatter and come back. It looked up at the noise and I held still with a stone in both hands. No nod either way, just a look, and then we both went back to work. Seven stones, two flat on both faces.
entries.title: Clack

entries.reason: a corner that rocks on its stone will throw the square I worked for
entries.text: Sighting across each stone beside the heap. Two sit dead flat, one rocks on a hump, one will do with a bed of gravel under it. That's three; the fourth corner wants one more trip.
entries.title: Flattest faces

entries.reason: the last corner wants a stone
entries.text: Back down to my shallows for one more, and found it under the second riffle: flat on both faces, a hand thick. The small one was on its log by its fire with a stick over the coals, something roasting; I could smell it across the water. It looked up when the stone clacked. I didn't stop, and neither did it.
entries.title: Fourth stone

queries: spirit level how to read the bubble
entries.query: spirit level how to read the bubble
entries.reason: There's a glass tube with a bubble in it in the chest and I've never once used it; if the sills sit on stones, the stones have to sit flat.
entries.source: Hunker: How To Read A Bubble Level
entries.text: Asked the tablet how to read the bubble in the long tool from the chest. Lay its edge flat, let the bubble settle, look at it with your eye level: between the two lines is level, nearer one line means that end sits high. Turn it end for end and the bubble should land in the same spot, or the tool itself is lying.
entries.title: The bubble tool

entries.text: The page only says lay it along. But a stone can sit level one way and tip the other, so every stone gets it twice, along and across. First I'll turn the tool end for end and see if it lies.
entries.title: Both ways

entries.text: Turned it end for end on the flattest stone: same spot both ways, so it tells the truth. Two stones read between the lines along and across, and the new one from the riffle sits true both ways. The rocker sends the bubble half out; it goes back to the creek. Three level and one to bed in gravel: that's four.
entries.title: Bubble says

entries.reason: Gravel's heavy work and the walk west is after it.
entries.text: A heel off the loaf and a wedge of cheese on the crate, slow, before the gravel. Across the water the small one is under the big trunk north of its fire again, bending for sticks; it saw me eating and went on picking. Left: a loaf less a heel, the cheese less three wedges, a ring and a quarter of sausage, oats less two fists, beans, most of the nuts and apples, salt, honey.
entries.title: Heel and wedge

entries.reason: The stones want a bed of gravel under them, and its fish don't want my noise.
entries.text: Down for gravel, and the small one is kneeling at its pool washing its hands; the water goes brown round them. Took the top end of my shallows, the farthest from it, and scraped up by the handful instead of tossing stones on a pile.
entries.title: Gravel, quiet

entries.text: Its fish stayed out the whole time, holding behind its big stone. It stayed too, crouched where I could see it, not hurrying. That's twice today we've both stayed. The gravel here is all worn round; I don't know yet if round packs.
entries.title: Its fish stayed

entries.onMind: scraping the corners to hard ground
entries.reason: Mark it before I dig, so I dig once.
entries.text: Tipped the first sackful down beside the stone heap; the corners will want three or four more. On the map sheet, a small ring of gravel round each of the four corner dots, and the rocker crossed out.
entries.title: Rings on the dots

queries: does round river gravel pack under a footing stone
entries.query: does round river gravel pack under a footing stone
entries.reason: Every bit of gravel in my shallows is worn round, and I don't want a corner I squared to drift.
entries.source: Hello Gravel: Crushed Stone for a Shed Base (vs River Rock)
entries.text: Asked whether round creek gravel packs under a footing. It doesn't, much: smooth faces don't interlock, so round stone shifts under load. Broken stone with sharp edges locks when you tamp it down in thin layers, a couple of inches at a time. Round is good for letting water run, not for holding weight.
entries.title: Round won't lock

entries.text: So my first sack is drainage, not footing. If it wants sharp stone, I break stone, and a hammer on rock rings a long way, all the way to its pool. That's a daylight problem for tomorrow.
entries.title: Drain, not footing

entries.reason: Last time I came back from the edge to a cold pit.
entries.text: Raked every bit of ash over the last embers and pushed the ring stones in before walking west. If a coal keeps till I'm back, no oil spent.
entries.title: Banked for the edge

entries.text: At my end of the stones the small one was crouched at its pool with its net flat in the water. Didn't step on; stood still with the map rolled under my arm. It lifted the net, empty, and held it up a bit at me. Dipped my head and went over slow, clogs set down flat; only one knock.
entries.title: I waited

entries.text: High thin cloud tonight, so the sun went into the sea pale orange instead of hard. Kept the box shut: ten is for a clear evening. No shore, no smoke, no sail, same as every night.
entries.title: Through the veil

entries.text: It held the net up so I'd see there was nothing in it yet. Like telling me I could go. Out here my people say the world stops, and back there something small is fishing and waiting on me to cross.
entries.title: Showed me empty

entries.reason: It showed me its empty net so I could cross; seemed right to show it something back.
entries.text: Came back by lantern. At the stones the small one was on its log by its fire, facing my way. Held the lantern up a little, the way it held up its net, and it watched me and didn't look away. Crossed with one knock.
entries.title: Lifted the lantern

entries.reason: Every lit wick is oil I don't get back.
entries.text: Raked the ash back: two coals still red under every bit of ash I had, an hour and a bit after banking. Shavings, two dry middles, one puff, and it stood up. Turned the lantern down to a bead and set it by the bench.
entries.title: A coal kept

entries.text: Two heels of bread and a long piece of sausage, sitting on the ground by my fire. Left: most of a loaf, the cheese less three wedges, about a ring of sausage, oats less two fists, the beans, most of the nuts and apples less one, salt, honey.
entries.title: Supper by my fire

entries.text: Two fires now, twenty paces apart with the water between. The small one is bent over something on its log by its own. Tomorrow I break stone, and a hammer on rock carries; better in the middle of the day, when its fish aren't biting anyway.
entries.title: Two fires

entries.text: Nightly needle check under the dome, hardly a breath of wind: swung, wobbled, settled on its scratch. The lever tail still slides on the step.
entries.title: Needle check

entries.reason: Firelight is free; the lantern stays a bead.
entries.text: Twisting stalk fiber by my fire. Over the water the small one sat on its log with a stick over its coals. Looked up and it was already looking my way; held it a breath, neither of us moved, then back to the twist.
entries.title: It was looking

entries.text: Two arm-lengths of two-ply cord off the stalks, even enough for a dropper line. Wet cord stretches, so it goes on the line dry.
entries.title: Two arm-lengths

entries.text: Wrote tomorrow on a squared page: break sharp stone at midday when its fish are down anyway; break with a hard creek cobble, not the claw hammer, whose face is for nails; lay it in thin layers and tamp each one.
entries.title: Stone, on paper

entries.reason: one middle now keeps it up till I turn in
entries.text: Laid a dry middle on and it caught clean. The low one did its five from upstream, and a long while later the high one answered. Over the water the small one sat dead still on its log, listening too.
entries.title: Both owls

entries.onMind: what the small one is cutting
entries.reason: the fish hold at different depths, and one bait only asks one of them
entries.text: Tied the new two-ply onto the fish line a hand above the bottom hook, so a second bait hangs higher in the water. Pulled every knot hard while the cord is dry; wet, it would stretch and slip.
entries.title: A dropper

entries.reason: it answered my lantern
entries.text: Looked over. The small one had put down whatever it was cutting and lifted its hand at me across the water, just a little. Took a breath and lifted mine back. Then we both went back to our hands.
entries.title: It lifted a hand

entries.text: I came here to be alone and I keep counting its fire. A lifted hand isn't asking anything. Maybe on this side of the water I'm not the one trespassing after all.
entries.title: Not trespassing, maybe

entries.reason: A stone that rings ought to be the hard one; a thud means it'll crumble first.
entries.text: Turned the flat stones from the footing heap over by firelight for a cobble to break with tomorrow. The dark gray one rings when I knock it on another; the brown ones thud. Over the water the small one sat with its head tipped back at the sky.
entries.title: One that rings

entries.reason: The keg runs out someday; pegs I can make from the woodpile.
entries.text: Whittling a peg from a split offcut with the short knife, tapered at one end, about as thick as the test hole. If a peg holds a joint, nails aren't the only way to fasten.
entries.title: A peg

entries.text: Over the water the small one sits bent over a pale square of light, like my tablet's, but at night. Mine's dead the minute the sun goes. What has it got that glows in the dark?
entries.title: A glow in its hands

entries.reason: A hammer carries at night, and it's reading.
entries.text: Tapped the peg into the crooked test hole with the hammer. On the third tap the small one looked up from its glow, so I kept it to three.
entries.title: Three taps

entries.text: The peg sits tight at the bottom of the hole and rocks at the top, because the burned hole is wider there. A peg wants a straight hole, and a burned one never is.
entries.title: Loose at the top

entries.reason: a burned hole is never straight
entries.text: Opened the chest by firelight and lifted out the bent crank and its row of bits in their slots. Fit the bit nearest my peg's thickness into its jaws and turned it against my palm. It wants to go round, not burn its way in.
entries.title: The crank with bits

entries.text: Over the water the small one is crouched at its ring, raking ash over the coals. About now every night its light goes down, and mine's still up.
entries.title: Its light goes down

entries.reason: firelight is free; oil is not
entries.text: Laid a split middle on and it took on the second breath, no smoke to speak of. Across the water its ring is a dark smudge now, and it has gone off toward its big tree.
entries.title: A split middle

entries.reason: find out what the crank is for
entries.text: Set the point on the offcut, leaned on the round head with my chest and cranked. The bit walked in and came out the far side in curls. I can sight straight through the hole at the fire: same width top and bottom.
entries.title: Straight through

entries.text: Tapped the peg in: tight at the mouth and tight at the bottom, and it won't rock. Kept it to a few soft taps; the small one has gone in to sleep.
entries.title: Tight all the way

entries.reason: so tomorrow starts where tonight ended
entries.text: Wrote it on a squared page: burned holes rock, cranked holes hold. Peg one sill corner in daylight, where I can watch the bit go in square.
entries.title: Written up

entries.reason: one peg alone lets the corner pivot
entries.text: Split the other half of the offcut and whittled it down to match the first peg. One peg in a lapped corner is only a hinge; two and it can't turn.
entries.title: A second peg

entries.text: Nightly needle check under the dome on a still, clear night: swung once, settled on its scratch.
entries.title: Needle check

entries.reason: a bed on an empty belly is a cold one
entries.text: A handful of nuts and one dried apple out of the bundle by the fire. Over the water its side is all dark now, not a spark in its ring.
entries.title: Nuts by the fire

entries.reason: a sill that slides spoils a straight hole
entries.text: Twisting dry stalk into two-ply on the fire's side. In daylight I want a sill lashed down to its footing stone while I bore, so it doesn't creep under the crank.
entries.title: Cord for the sills

entries.reason: warm hands sleep easier than cold ones
entries.text: Hands out to the fire before I bury it. The low one did its five from upstream and nothing answered. Over the water nothing moves; its side has been dark an hour.
entries.title: Hands to it

entries.reason: two pegs in one corner should be twins
entries.text: Sighted down both pegs against the flames. The second runs a hair fatter at the head than the first; a scrape in daylight and they will match. They go in holes from the same bit, so they had better.
entries.title: A hair fat

entries.reason: a kept coal is cheaper than a lit wick
entries.text: Set the two half-burned sticks aside for the morning and heaped every bit of ash over the coals, then pushed the ring stones in. Last time that kept two coals; tomorrow should start without a drop of oil.
entries.title: Buried for morning

moves.doing: nudging the floating needle in the tin lid under the glass dome on the bench
moves.goal: make the nightly check that the needle still settles on its scratch

moves.doing: twisting dead stalk fiber into cord, sitting by his fire
moves.goal: have fresh line for the fish and lashing, using the firelight instead of oil

moves.doing: writing in his notebook with the pencil by his fire
moves.goal: set down how he will break sharp stone tomorrow before he forgets it

moves.doing: laying a dry split middle on his fire
moves.goal: keep the fire standing for the rest of the evening

moves.doing: tying the new stalk cord onto his fish line as a dropper, sitting by his fire
moves.goal: have a second hook hanging higher in the water for tomorrow, using firelight instead of oil

moves.doing: sitting by his fire with his hands to the flames
moves.goal: warm through and settle before more work

moves.doing: turning over flat creek stones from the footing heap by firelight
moves.goal: pick a hard cobble to break sharp stone with tomorrow

moves.doing: whittling a tapered peg from a split offcut with the short knife, sitting by his fire
moves.goal: see whether a wooden peg could hold a joint instead of a nail

moves.doing: sitting by his fire with his hands to the flames, looking across the water
moves.goal: warm his hands before the fitting

moves.doing: tapping the whittled peg into the test hole in the offcut with the hammer at the bench
moves.goal: find out whether the peg fits tight in a burned hole

moves.doing: lifting the crank tool and its bits out of the tool chest and turning them over by firelight
moves.goal: find something in the chest that bores a straight hole

moves.doing: laying a split middle on his fire
moves.goal: keep the fire up to work by instead of burning oil

moves.doing: sighting through a fresh straight hole in the offcut at the bench, then tapping a peg into it with the hammer
moves.goal: see whether a peg holds tight in a straight hole

moves.doing: writing in his notebook with the pencil, sitting by his fire
moves.goal: set down what the crank tool taught him before he forgets it

moves.doing: whittling a second peg from the other half of the split offcut with a carving knife, sitting by his fire
moves.goal: have a second peg ready so tomorrow's corner can't turn on a single one

moves.doing: nudging the floating needle in its tin lid under the glass dome at the bench
moves.goal: do the nightly needle check before bed

moves.doing: eating a handful of nuts and a dried apple from the food bundle, sitting by his fire
moves.goal: put something in his belly so he doesn't go to bed hungry

moves.doing: twisting dry stalk fibers into cord, sitting by his fire
moves.goal: have cord ready to lash a sill to the footing stones in daylight

moves.doing: sitting by his fire with his hands held out to it
moves.goal: warm his hands through before he buries the fire for the night

moves.doing: holding the two pegs up to the firelight by his fire and sighting along each one
moves.goal: check the two pegs match before they go into the same corner

moves.doing: raking ash over the coals of his fire pit and pushing the ring stones in
moves.goal: keep a coal alive under the ash so the morning fire costs no oil
